evidence.title: Dietary supplement use and recommendations for discontinuation in an integrative oncology clinic.
evidence.authors: D'Andre SD; Bauer BA; Hofmann MB; Burckhard JL; Montane HN; Loprinzi CL
evidence.venue: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_9: In 35% of patients, we recommended stopping some of their DS or other therapies, the reasons being: DC antioxidants, vitamin B12/iron while on chemo/RT (unless deficient or part of protocol) 32%; DC due to taking excess amounts (i.e., fat-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron) 13.5%; DC supplements with known toxicity (i.e., laetrile, Miracle mineral solution) 13.5%; DC due to interactions with other medications (i.e., anticoagulants) 13.5%; DC DS with potential to increase cancer growth (i.e., estrogenic potential in those with hormone-sensitive cancers, glutamine) 11%; DC due to potential for increased toxicity with chemotherapy (i.e., increased risk of bleeding, CIPN) 11%; DC probiotics, immune stimulants, and cannabis while on immunotherapy 5.4%.
evidence.outcome: There is potential for harm in several ways: (1) interactions with their medications that may increase side effects, (2) interactions with their treatment that may lead to decreased efficacy, and 3) direct toxicity from the supplement. | In 35% of patients, we recommended stopping some of their DS or other therapies, the reasons being: DC antioxidants, vitamin B12/iron while on chemo/RT (unless deficient or part of protocol) 32%; DC due to taking excess amounts (i.e., fat-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron) 13.5%; DC supplements with known toxicity (i.e., laetrile, Miracle mineral solution) 13.5%; DC due to interactions with other medications (i.e., anticoagulants) 13.5%; DC DS with potential to increase cancer growth (i.e., estrogenic potential in those with hormone-sensitive cancers, glutamine) 11%; DC due to potential for increased toxicity with chemotherapy (i.e., increased risk of bleeding, CIPN) 11%; DC probiotics, immune stimulants, and cannabis while on immunotherapy 5.4%. | CONCLUSIONS: Patients with cancer referred to an integrative oncology clinic use large numbers of DS with the potential for adverse effects and/or decreasing efficacy of treatments.
evidence.key_finding: In 35% of patients, we recommended stopping some of their DS or other therapies, the reasons being: DC antioxidants, vitamin B12/iron while on chemo/RT (unless deficient or part of protocol) 32%; DC due to taking excess amounts (i.e., fat-soluble vitamins, calcium, iron) 13.5%; DC supplements with known toxicity (i.e., laetrile, Miracle mineral solution) 13.5%; DC due to interactions with other medications (i.e., anticoagulants) 13.5%; DC DS with potential to increase cancer growth (i.e., estrogenic potential in those with hormone-sensitive cancers, glutamine) 11%; DC due to potential for increased toxicity with chemotherapy (i.e., increased risk of bleeding, CIPN) 11%; DC probiotics, immune stimulants, and cannabis while on immunotherapy 5.4%.
evidence.key_finding_ko: 환자의 35%에게 일부 식이 보충제(DS) 또는 다른 치료의 중단을 권고했다. 중단(DC) 사유는 항암화학요법/방사선치료 중 항산화제, 비타민 B12/철분 사용(결핍이 있거나 치료 프로토콜에 포함된 경우 제외) 32%, 과량 복용(예: 지용성 비타민, 칼슘, 철분) 13.5%, 독성이 알려진 보충제(예: 레트릴, Miracle mineral solution) 13.5%, 다른 약물(예: 항응고제)과의 상호작용 13.5%, 암 성장을 촉진할 가능성이 있는 식이 보충제(예: 호르몬 민감성 암 환자에서 에스트로겐성 가능성이 있는 보충제, 글루타민) 11%, 항암화학요법 독성을 증가시킬 가능성(예: 출혈 위험 증가, CIPN) 11%, 면역요법 중 프로바이오틱스·면역 자극제·대마 사용 5.4%였다.

evidence.title: Interactions of commonly used dietary supplements with cardiovascular drugs: a systematic review.
evidence.authors: Kanji S; Seely D; Yazdi F; Tetzlaff J; Singh K; Tsertsvadze A; Tricco AC; Sears ME; Ooi TC; Turek MA; Skidmore B; Ansari MT
evidence.locator:
ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_10: Incremental benefits were noted for triglyceridemia with omega-3 fatty acid added to statins; and there was an improvement in levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol with garlic supplementation when people also consumed nitrates
CONCLUSIONS: Evidence of low-strength indicates benefits of omega-3 fatty acids (plus statin, or calcium channel blockers and antiplatelets) and garlic (plus nitrates or warfarin) on triglycerides and HDL-C, respectively.
evidence.outcome: BACKGROUND: The objective of this systematic review was to examine the benefits, harms and pharmacokinetic interactions arising from the co-administration of commonly used dietary supplements with cardiovascular drugs. | Many patients on cardiovascular drugs take dietary supplements for presumed benefits and may be at risk for adverse supplement-drug interactions. | With only a few small studies available per supplement, evidence was insufficient for all predefined gradable clinical efficacy and harms outcomes, such as mortality and serious adverse events.
evidence.key_finding:
Incremental benefits were noted for triglyceridemia with omega-3 fatty acid added to statins; and there was an improvement in levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol with garlic supplementation when people also consumed nitrates
CONCLUSIONS: Evidence of low-strength indicates benefits of omega-3 fatty acids (plus statin, or calcium channel blockers and antiplatelets) and garlic (plus nitrates or warfarin) on triglycerides and HDL-C, respectively.
evidence.key_finding_ko: 스타틴에 오메가-3 지방산을 추가했을 때 중성지방혈증에 대한 추가 이점이 관찰되었고, 질산염도 섭취한 사람에서는 마늘 보충제를 복용했을 때 고밀도 지단백 콜레스테롤 수치가 개선되었다. 결론: 강도가 낮은 근거에 따르면 오메가-3 지방산(스타틴 또는 칼슘 통로 차단제 및 항혈소판제와 병용)과 마늘(질산염 또는 와파린과 병용)은 각각 중성지방과 HDL-C에 이점이 있다.

evidence.title: Vitamin K supplementation can improve stability of anticoagulation for patients with unexplained variability in response to warfarin.
evidence.authors: Sconce E; Avery P; Wynne H; Kamali F
evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_5: Vitamin K supplementation resulted in a significantly greater decrease in standard deviation of international normalized ratio (INR) compared with placebo (-0.24 +/- 0.14 vs -0.11 +/- 0.18; P < .001) and a significantly greater increase in percentage time within target INR range (28% +/- 20% vs 15% +/- 20%; P < .01).
evidence.outcome: Patients receiving warfarin who have unstable control of anticoagulation have a significantly lower intake of dietary vitamin K compared with their stable counterparts. | We hypothesized that supplementation with oral vitamin K would improve stability in patients with previously unstable control of anticoagulation. | Seventy warfarin-treated patients with unstable anticoagulation control were randomly assigned in a double-blinded fashion to receive a daily amount of 150 mug oral vitamin K or placebo orally for 6 months.
evidence.key_finding: Vitamin K supplementation resulted in a significantly greater decrease in standard deviation of international normalized ratio (INR) compared with placebo (-0.24 +/- 0.14 vs -0.11 +/- 0.18; P < .001) and a significantly greater increase in percentage time within target INR range (28% +/- 20% vs 15% +/- 20%; P < .01).
evidence.key_finding_ko: 비타민 K 보충군은 위약군보다 국제정상화비율(INR) 표준편차가 유의하게 더 크게 감소했고(-0.24 +/- 0.14 vs -0.11 +/- 0.18; P < .001), 목표 INR 범위 안에 있었던 시간의 비율도 유의하게 더 크게 증가했다(28% +/- 20% vs 15% +/- 20%; P < .01).
evidence.population: Patients receiving warfarin who have unstable control of anticoagulation have a significantly lower intake of dietary vitamin K compared with their stable counterparts. | We hypothesized that supplementation with oral vitamin K would improve stability in patients with previously unstable control of anticoagulation. | Seventy warfarin-treated patients with unstable anticoagulation control were randomly assigned in a double-blinded fashion to receive a daily amount of 150 mug oral vitamin K or placebo orally for 6 months.

evidence.title: Over-the-counter vitamin K1-containing multivitamin supplements disrupt warfarin anticoagulation in vitamin K1-depleted patients. A prospective, controlled trial.
evidence.authors: Kurnik D; Loebstein R; Rabinovitz H; Austerweil N; Halkin H; Almog S
evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_11: We conclude that vitamin K(1)-containing multivitamins reduce INR in patients with low vitamin K(1) status.
evidence.outcome: Most multivitamin supplements contain far less vitamin K(1) than thought to affect warfarin anticoagulation. | Having described 3 patients with multivitamin-warfarin interactions, we hypothesized that vitamin K(1)-depleted patients are sensitive to even small increments. | Therefore, we compared the effect of a vitamin K(1)-containing multivitamin on warfarin anticoagulation between patients with low versus normal vitamin K(1) status.
evidence.key_finding: We conclude that vitamin K(1)-containing multivitamins reduce INR in patients with low vitamin K(1) status.
evidence.key_finding_ko: 비타민 K(1)이 함유된 종합비타민은 비타민 K(1) 상태가 낮은 환자의 INR을 낮춘다고 결론지었다.
evidence.population: Most multivitamin supplements contain far less vitamin K(1) than thought to affect warfarin anticoagulation. | Having described 3 patients with multivitamin-warfarin interactions, we hypothesized that vitamin K(1)-depleted patients are sensitive to even small increments. | Therefore, we compared the effect of a vitamin K(1)-containing multivitamin on warfarin anticoagulation between patients with low versus normal vitamin K(1) status.

all_evidence.title: Prospective study of supplemental vitamin K therapy in patients on oral anticoagulants with unstable international normalized ratios.
all_evidence.authors: Ford SK; Misita CP; Shilliday BB; Malone RM; Moore CG; Moll S
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_6: RESULTS: Vitamin K supplementation led to a decrease in INR variability in five of the nine patients studied (56%).
all_evidence.outcome: We sought to determine whether vitamin K supplementation may decrease INR variability in patients with a history of unstable INRs, how soon the INR decreases after vitamin K therapy is initiated, the time to reach a therapeutic INR after vitamin K initiation, and how much of an increase in oral anticoagulant dose is needed to maintain the INR in the desired range. | RESULTS: Vitamin K supplementation led to a decrease in INR variability in five of the nine patients studied (56%). | INR decrease occurred 2-7 days after initiation of vitamin K.
all_evidence.key_finding: RESULTS: Vitamin K supplementation led to a decrease in INR variability in five of the nine patients studied (56%).

all_evidence.publication_types: Controlled Clinical Trial|Journal Article|Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't
all_evidence.population: We sought to determine whether vitamin K supplementation may decrease INR variability in patients with a history of unstable INRs, how soon the INR decreases after vitamin K therapy is initiated, the time to reach a therapeutic INR after vitamin K initiation, and how much of an increase in oral anticoagulant dose is needed to maintain the INR in the desired range. | METHODS: This is a prospective open label crossover study of patients on warfarin with a history of fluctuating INRs. | Therapeutic INRs were achieved 2-35 days after vitamin K therapy was initiated and an increase in warfarin dose of 6-95% was required to bring the INR back into the therapeutic range.

all_evidence.title: Interaction Between Dietary Vitamin K Intake and Anticoagulation by Vitamin K Antagonists: Is It Really True?: A Systematic Review.
all_evidence.authors: Violi F; Lip GY; Pignatelli P; Pastori D
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_4: We excluded all studies of supplementation of vitamin K alone.We performed a systematic review of the literature up to October 2015, searching for a combination of "food," "diet," "vitamin K," "phylloquinone," "warfarin," "INR," "coagulation," and "anticoagulant."Two dietary interventional trials and 9 observational studies were included.
all_evidence.outcome: Common belief is that dietary vitamin K intake could counteract the anticoagulant effect by VKAs and for many years, patients have been discouraged to consume vitamin-K-rich foods, such as green leafy vegetables.The objective of this study is to summarize the current evidence supporting the putative interaction between dietary vitamin K intake and changes in INR with the VKAs.Data sources are MEDLINE via PubMed and Cochrane database.All clinical studies investigating the relationship between dietary vitamin K and measures of anticoagulation were included. | We excluded all studies of supplementation of vitamin K alone.We performed a systematic review of the literature up to October 2015, searching for a combination of "food," "diet," "vitamin K," "phylloquinone," "warfarin," "INR," "coagulation," and "anticoagulant."Two dietary interventional trials and 9 observational studies were included. | We found conflicting evidence on the effect of dietary intake of vitamin K on coagulation response.
all_evidence.key_finding: We excluded all studies of supplementation of vitamin K alone.We performed a systematic review of the literature up to October 2015, searching for a combination of "food," "diet," "vitamin K," "phylloquinone," "warfarin," "INR," "coagulation," and "anticoagulant."Two dietary interventional trials and 9 observational studies were included.

all_evidence.title: Potential glucosamine-warfarin interaction resulting in increased international normalized ratio: case report and review of the literature and MedWatch database.
all_evidence.authors: Knudsen JF; Sokol GH
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_10: Using the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) MedWatch database, 20 reports of glucosamine or glucosamine-chondroitin sulfate use with warfarin associated with altered coagulation (manifested by increased INR, or increased bleeding or bruising) were identified.
all_evidence.outcome: We describe a 71-year-old man who had received warfarin 7.5 mg/day for 5 years for atrial fibrillation, which had maintained his international normalized ratio (INR) within a narrow range of 2.5-3.2. | The patient then increased his dosage of glucosamine to 1500 mg and chondroitin to 1200 mg twice/day; his INR previous to this change was 2.3. | Approximately 3 weeks later, his INR increased to 3.9.
all_evidence.key_finding: Using the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) MedWatch database, 20 reports of glucosamine or glucosamine-chondroitin sulfate use with warfarin associated with altered coagulation (manifested by increased INR, or increased bleeding or bruising) were identified.
all_evidence.key_finding_ko: 미국 식품의약국(FDA) MedWatch 데이터베이스를 이용해, 응고 변화(INR 증가 또는 출혈이나 멍 증가로 나타남)와 관련하여 와파린과 글루코사민 또는 글루코사민-콘드로이틴 황산염을 함께 사용한 보고 20건을 확인했다.
all_evidence.population: We describe a 71-year-old man who had received warfarin 7.5 mg/day for 5 years for atrial fibrillation, which had maintained his international normalized ratio (INR) within a narrow range of 2.5-3.2. | The supplement was then stopped, and his warfarin schedule was changed to 7.5 mg every other day alternating with 3.75 mg every other day. | This case report suggests that a potential interaction exists between warfarin and glucosamine that is associated with an increase in the INR.

all_evidence.title: Drug and dietary interactions of the new and emerging oral anticoagulants.
all_evidence.authors: Walenga JM; Adiguzel C
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_1: Oral warfarin is associated with extensive food and drug interactions, and there is a need to consider such interactions with the new oral anticoagulants (OACs) dabigatran etexilate, rivaroxaban and apixaban.
all_evidence.outcome: Oral warfarin is associated with extensive food and drug interactions, and there is a need to consider such interactions with the new oral anticoagulants (OACs) dabigatran etexilate, rivaroxaban and apixaban. | A literature survey was conducted using PubMed, EMBASE and recent abstracts from thrombosis meetings to identify publications related to food, drug and dietary supplement interaction studies with dabigatran etexilate, rivaroxaban and apixaban. | Clinical experience regarding food interactions is currently limited.
all_evidence.key_finding: Oral warfarin is associated with extensive food and drug interactions, and there is a need to consider such interactions with the new oral anticoagulants (OACs) dabigatran etexilate, rivaroxaban and apixaban.

all_evidence.title: Clinically relevant interaction between warfarin and scuppernongs, a quercetin containing muscadine grape: continued questions surrounding flavonoid-induced warfarin interactions.
all_evidence.authors: Woodward CJ; Deyo ZM; Donahue KE; Deal AM; Hawes EM
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_1: We present a case of clinically relevant and probable interaction between warfarin and scuppernongs in a 73-year-old woman where ingestion of scuppernongs, a variety of quercetin-containing muscadine grapes, over a period of 2 months was associated with elevations in the International Normalised Ratio to supratherapeutic levels.

all_evidence.title: Analysis of Factors That Interrupt With INR Control in the First Anticoagulation Clinic Monitoring Jordanian Patients.
all_evidence.authors: Al-Momany NH; Makahleh ZM; Al-Omari NA; Al-Sarayreh HA; Momani RO
all_evidence.venue: Clinical and applied thrombosis/hemostasis : official journal of the International Academy of Clinical and Applied Thrombosis/Hemostasis
all_evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_17: Factors that interrupted INR control in our population, arranged in descending sequence, were concurrent medication use 46.9% (mainly Salicylates and Amiodarone), smoking cigarettes and shisha 17% (represented the most frequent single factor that caused non-TINR in the present study), a nonbalanced dietary vitamin K intake 16.88% caused changes in INR (lower) was related to an increase in the intake of vitamin K-rich food, were noticed to be much more in the spring season in Jordan (end of March and April mainly), herbal supplements 15.02%; Hawthorn (Crataegus, الزعرور) is an herb that lives widely in Jordan, and shockingly we found that it is used very commonly in our ACC patients and corresponded to an elevated INR <8 in 11 patients, and serious bleeding events that required hospitalization in 2 cases), noncompliance 1.49%, comorbid diseases 1%, malabsorption 0.53%, alcohol intake 0.39%, and VKORC1 A/G and CYP2C9 *1*1 genotype 0.15%.
all_evidence.outcome: Multiple factors such as vitamin K consumption, drug interactions, herbs interactions, disease states, and alcohol intake affect international normalized ratio (INR) values and thus warfarin dosing. | In contrast, the factors that affect INR control in a specific population are rarely studied. | Being aware of these factors contributes a lot in maintaining an INR control and avoiding the supratherapeutic or subtherapeutic anticoagulation and the associated risks of hemorrhage or thromboembolism.
all_evidence.key_finding: Factors that interrupted INR control in our population, arranged in descending sequence, were concurrent medication use 46.9% (mainly Salicylates and Amiodarone), smoking cigarettes and shisha 17% (represented the most frequent single factor that caused non-TINR in the present study), a nonbalanced dietary vitamin K intake 16.88% caused changes in INR (lower) was related to an increase in the intake of vitamin K-rich food, were noticed to be much more in the spring season in Jordan (end of March and April mainly), herbal supplements 15.02%; Hawthorn (Crataegus, الزعرور) is an herb that lives widely in Jordan, and shockingly we found that it is used very commonly in our ACC patients and corresponded to an elevated INR <8 in 11 patients, and serious bleeding events that required hospitalization in 2 cases), noncompliance 1.49%, comorbid diseases 1%, malabsorption 0.53%, alcohol intake 0.39%, and VKORC1 A/G and CYP2C9 *1*1 genotype 0.15%.
all_evidence.key_finding_ko: 연구 대상 집단에서 INR 조절을 방해한 요인을 빈도 내림차순으로 배열하면 병용 약물 사용 46.9%(주로 살리실산염과 아미오다론), 담배와 시샤 흡연 17%(본 연구에서 비목표 INR을 유발한 가장 흔한 단일 요인), 불균형한 식이 비타민 K 섭취 16.88%였다. 비타민 K가 풍부한 음식 섭취 증가와 관련해 INR이 낮아졌으며, 이는 요르단의 봄철(주로 삼월 말과 사월)에 훨씬 더 많이 관찰되었다. 허브 보충제는 15.02%였다. 산사나무(Crataegus, الزعرور)는 요르단 전역에 자라는 허브로, 놀랍게도 항응고 클리닉 환자들이 매우 흔히 사용했으며 환자 11명에서 INR <8 상승과 관련되었고, 2건에서는 입원이 필요한 중대한 출혈이 발생했다. 그 밖의 요인은 복약 불이행 1.49%, 동반 질환 1%, 흡수 장애 0.53%, 음주 0.39%, VKORC1 A/G 및 CYP2C9 *1*1 유전자형 0.15%였다.
all_evidence.population: Multiple factors such as vitamin K consumption, drug interactions, herbs interactions, disease states, and alcohol intake affect international normalized ratio (INR) values and thus warfarin dosing. | Being aware of these factors contributes a lot in maintaining an INR control and avoiding the supratherapeutic or subtherapeutic anticoagulation and the associated risks of hemorrhage or thromboembolism. | Alarming factors causing non-TINR detected in our study include smoking both cigarettes and shisha, herbal use (Hawthorn and Ginseng), increased intake of vitamin K rich food in the spring season, and concurrent medication use (Salicylates, Amiodarone, Ciprofloxacin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDS], Azithromycin, Clarithromycin: although the use of these drugs is mandatory sometimes, it can be replaced by an alternative, eg, antibiotics or monitored closely together with warfarin).

evidence.title: Interactions of commonly used dietary supplements with cardiovascular drugs: a systematic review.
evidence.authors: Kanji S; Seely D; Yazdi F; Tetzlaff J; Singh K; Tsertsvadze A; Tricco AC; Sears ME; Ooi TC; Turek MA; Skidmore B; Ansari MT
evidence.locator:
ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_10: Incremental benefits were noted for triglyceridemia with omega-3 fatty acid added to statins; and there was an improvement in levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol with garlic supplementation when people also consumed nitrates
CONCLUSIONS: Evidence of low-strength indicates benefits of omega-3 fatty acids (plus statin, or calcium channel blockers and antiplatelets) and garlic (plus nitrates or warfarin) on triglycerides and HDL-C, respectively.
evidence.outcome: BACKGROUND: The objective of this systematic review was to examine the benefits, harms and pharmacokinetic interactions arising from the co-administration of commonly used dietary supplements with cardiovascular drugs. | Many patients on cardiovascular drugs take dietary supplements for presumed benefits and may be at risk for adverse supplement-drug interactions. | With only a few small studies available per supplement, evidence was insufficient for all predefined gradable clinical efficacy and harms outcomes, such as mortality and serious adverse events.
evidence.key_finding:
Incremental benefits were noted for triglyceridemia with omega-3 fatty acid added to statins; and there was an improvement in levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol with garlic supplementation when people also consumed nitrates
CONCLUSIONS: Evidence of low-strength indicates benefits of omega-3 fatty acids (plus statin, or calcium channel blockers and antiplatelets) and garlic (plus nitrates or warfarin) on triglycerides and HDL-C, respectively.
evidence.key_finding_ko: 스타틴에 오메가-3 지방산을 추가했을 때 중성지방혈증에 대한 추가 이점이 관찰되었고, 질산염도 섭취한 사람에서는 마늘 보충제를 복용했을 때 고밀도 지단백 콜레스테롤 수치가 개선되었다. 결론: 강도가 낮은 근거에 따르면 오메가-3 지방산(스타틴 또는 칼슘 통로 차단제 및 항혈소판제와 병용)과 마늘(질산염 또는 와파린과 병용)은 각각 중성지방과 HDL-C에 이점이 있다.

evidence.title: Impact of vitamin D supplementation on arterial vasomotion, stiffness and endothelial biomarkers in chronic kidney disease patients.
evidence.authors: Chitalia N; Ismail T; Tooth L; Boa F; Hampson G; Goldsmith D; Kaski JC; Banerjee D
evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_10: CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates for the first time improvement of endothelial vasomotor and secretory functions with vitamin D in CKD patients without significant adverse effects on arterial stiffness, serum calcium or FGF-23.
evidence.outcome: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular events are frequent and vascular endothelial function is abnormal in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). | CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates for the first time improvement of endothelial vasomotor and secretory functions with vitamin D in CKD patients without significant adverse effects on arterial stiffness, serum calcium or FGF-23.
evidence.key_finding: CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates for the first time improvement of endothelial vasomotor and secretory functions with vitamin D in CKD patients without significant adverse effects on arterial stiffness, serum calcium or FGF-23.
evidence.key_finding_ko: 결론: 이 연구는 동맥 경직도, 혈청 칼슘 또는 FGF-23에 유의한 이상 영향을 주지 않으면서 비타민 D가 CKD 환자의 내피 혈관운동 기능과 분비 기능을 개선한다는 점을 처음으로 입증했다.
evidence.publication_types: Clinical Trial|Journal Article|Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't
evidence.population: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular events are frequent and vascular endothelial function is abnormal in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). | We demonstrated endothelial dysfunction with vitamin D deficiency in CKD patients; however the impact of cholecalciferol supplementation on vascular stiffness and vasomotor function, endothelial and bone biomarkers in CKD patients with low 25-hydroxy vitamin D [25(OH)D] is unknown, which this study investigated. | METHODS: We assessed non-diabetic patients with CKD stage 3/4, age 17-80 years and serum 25(OH)D <75 nmol/L.

evidence.title: Vitamin K for Vascular Calcification in Kidney Patients: Still Alive and Kicking, but Still a Lot to Learn.

evidence.locator: ABSTRACT_SENTENCE_2: Vascular calcification (VC) is the result of an ongoing process of misplaced calcium in the inner and medial layers of the arteries, which has emerged as a critical contributor to cardiovascular events in CKD.
evidence.outcome: Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) suffer disproportionately from a high burden of cardiovascular disease, which, despite recent scientific advances, remains partly understood. | Vascular calcification (VC) is the result of an ongoing process of misplaced calcium in the inner and medial layers of the arteries, which has emerged as a critical contributor to cardiovascular events in CKD.
evidence.key_finding: Vascular calcification (VC) is the result of an ongoing process of misplaced calcium in the inner and medial layers of the arteries, which has emerged as a critical contributor to cardiovascular events in CKD.

evidence.population: Patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) suffer disproportionately from a high burden of cardiovascular disease, which, despite recent scientific advances, remains partly understood. | Vascular calcification (VC) is the result of an ongoing process of misplaced calcium in the inner and medial layers of the arteries, which has emerged as a critical contributor to cardiovascular events in CKD. | CKD patients, especially in advanced stages, often present with vitamin K deficiency due to dietary restrictions, medications, and impaired intestinal absorption in the uremic environment.
